title: Why, and How To, Walk the World
subtitle: Additional thoughts after five years
contentHtml:
I started this newsletter with two how-to articles — on walking and traveling — but it’s now over five years old, and since newsletters age like dogs, it's now in its late thirties: old enough to feel wiser. While I’ve not changed my core philosophy, the logistics of how I do both have evolved.

What is that core philosophy? There are two principles. The first is that by immersing yourself in the physical world you learn in ways that you cannot by simply reading, and the most effective way to do that is to walk. Not along secluded trails through nature, but across cities, regions, and even nations, because that’s where the people are. While I’m all for the solitary stroll through the sublime, my primary interest is in culture, and culture is shaped by humans more than geography, and I want to be around them.

So rather than take on the Appalachian Trail, I walk across Jakarta, or Amman, or from Dortmund to Cologne, or the width of England through its old industrial belt — to engage with each on a human scale, as the citizens do. That means spending considerable time in the boring or uncomfortable bits most outsiders fast-forward through, or over — the dreary council housing estates in the UK, the concrete Khrushchyovkas in former Soviet nations, the slums swelling with aspirational arrivals in third-world megacities, and then the decaying villages they came from.

There’s a lot of blandness and blight on that list, intentionally so. That's where a region's culture is strongest, most genuine, and where you learn the most. They don’t exist for the outsider, and are not self-aware in the way show neighborhoods are.

Those show neighborhoods — the enclaves with museums, fine dining, and well-to-do homes — are great for several days, but they are not my primary focus because they’re all too similar. They’re where globalism has had the greatest impact, and while they are obviously not exact replicas of each other — Mayfair in London is clearly not a copy of Palermo in Buenos Aires — the citizens1 of both could swap places with little discomfort, or cultural shock beyond things such as “they eat later here.” And many of the differences that do exist are curated for show, exaggerated affectations of authenticity. Simply put, wealth has a leveling effect that limits what you can learn while traveling.

The second core principle is that walking is conducive to your well-being, in a holistic sense. I used to be a runner, the type to get up at 4:30 am to pound out five miles before work, and I remember exactly when it struck me this wasn’t healthy. I was under the BQE in Brooklyn near the end of my route and I’d just stepped in a greasy puddle and I stopped to drain my shoe and while I was sitting on the curb, semis chugging past in the first morning light, my face contorted in pain, my shins throbbing, my toes blistering, I realized I’d probably run over 45,000 miles since my birth and that was enough medicinal torture for one lifetime. Whatever this was doing for me, it was no longer my route to contentment.

That’s when I shifted to walking, which is far easier on the body2, and stimulates thoughts other than “when will this end?” Some people get their ideas in the shower, I get them walking, which is why if you’re driving near New Paltz, NY, you might see a scraggly guy in bright orange work-gear jotting notes down by the side of the road.

Walking is meditative, and while I’m not much of an evolutionary biologist, that could be because that’s how we are built — to endure, rather than to be fast. Almost all animals our size can beat us in a 100-yard dash, but very few can match us over long distances. We are built to constantly move at a walking pace — and reading history, it’s remarkable how commonplace what we now consider epic walks were. Pilgrimages, armies on the move, whole populations forced to relocate thousands of miles, and it’s only in the last century that this has stopped. Well, not completely.

When I was in Kampala I landed with the naive idea I’d walk to the Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs, ten miles from my hotel, but because of atrocious infrastructure I discovered it was longer than that. Eventually I had to give up because I was covered in mud, close to heat exhaustion, and tired of the diesel fumes. I took a boda-boda3 the rest of the way, and felt something of a hero that I’d made it as far as I had. After mass I saw that the grounds of the shrine were effectively a campsite for hundreds of families, all with their possessions in large cloth sacks. I talked to some of them, a mix of pilgrims and refugees who’d all walked some six hundred miles from the Congo. Any notions of my heroism immediately melted into a deep humility.

So much for the big picture; now to details on how to walk the world. For context, here are four prior pieces. The first two, heavy on logistics (what I wear, etc.), are over four years old, but I still agree with most of what’s in them.

  • How to Travel

  • How to Walk

  • Thick Travel

  • Why and how to walk 200 miles

This is very inside-baseball-y but I do get asked these questions so often and wanted to put them all in a single post.

What’s your favorite place?

When people find out I’m a travel writer they immediately ask, “So, what’s your favorite place?” and I used to hem and haw and say, "Well, depends on if you mean…” and now I simply say Japan, which is close enough to the truth to keep me out of the confessional. No matter what you’re looking for as a tourist — cultural riches, fantastic food, sublime nature, a sense of dislocation without a hint of trauma, fun nightlife — Japan is at or near the top. After saying that I will add, because I can’t help myself, that they should try to get out of central Tokyo, even if that means jumping on a subway and riding forty minutes in any direction. Then if still interested, I’ll tell them the real trick is to go someplace even further removed, like Kumamoto, where you get 90% of what you get from Tokyo without a whiff of over-tourism, except for buses of Chinese on buying-useless-stuff vacations.

My more nuanced response is to ask “What are you looking for?” and if the answer is “something different and unconventional” then it’s anywhere in Central Asia, especially Mongolia, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan, which have stunning natural beauty while also being about as different as the modern world allows. They are some of the last places with a remoteness (physically and culturally) that once was the hallmark of all travel. If the answer is “A place to move with my family to, or retire in” then my answer is somewhere in Australia (Sydney, Perth, Brisbane), Japan (Kyushu), the South of France, or Lombardy, although honestly I will probably always live in the US.

As open-minded as I am, as experiential, I’m still a product of my own culture, and so the US is where I’m most comfortable.

How do you choose where to go?

I've got no discernible method for choosing where I visit. At this point it's largely intuitive, driven by my mood, past experiences, and whatever rabbit-hole I've been going down in my reading.

I suppose if I had to put it into a formula it would be trying to maximize

.4x + .3y + .2z + .1v

with x = what I expect to learn, y = comfort, z = whim of the moment, and v = novelty. Or, I put learning and comfort over being in a place to say I’ve been in that place.

I’m not a pins-in-the-map man, trying to visit every country. I run into plenty of those and while that could be a bias-free algorithm to maximize the unexpected, I’ve found turning travel into a complete-it-all quest ends up becoming manic and all-consuming.

I usually have large themes that I’m working through — initially it was about faith, so I focused on Muslim countries because I knew less about that, and then it became about how elites construct culture (inspired by a short stay in Shanghai), so I shifted towards ping-ponging between the US, East Asia, and Europe, each with a different model of liberalism, or a rejection of it (China).

But again, there’s little method here, and I’m constantly jotting notes down on where to visit based on what I’m reading, or the hours I spend looking at maps, airline routes, bus schedules, and so on.

Here is my current list, each entry inspired by something different, what exactly I’m not sure.

  • Kigali

  • Yorkshire long walk

  • New Zealand by bus

  • Northern Scandinavia by bus in June

  • Argentina by bus (Comodoro Rivadavia)

  • Bologna to Padua long walk

  • Indonesia again (focus outside Java)

  • Namibia (May?)

  • Africa’s Cup Tournament (Uganda again)

  • Shetlands

  • Baku/Dushanbe

  • Belarus

  • Bay Area long walk

  • Turkmenistan

  • Imjin War trip (Japan to Korea with stops in Iki, Tsushima, Hansando, etc.)

  • Bus trip across Canada

My five-week trip that begins this Saturday is an example of my scattershot approach. I have a weekend conference (on Midwestern studies4) in Sioux Falls, SD, and rather than fly in, fly out, confined to a downtown hotel, which felt contrary to the point, I’m taking a bus to Sioux Falls (from Minneapolis) to spend several days out at the Walmart plaza first. While downtown revitalization is a worthy thing happening in mid-sized communities, another reality is that the conglomeration of franchises that lies adjacent to interstates has become a new downtown. You cannot talk about the Midwest if you ignore them.

After the conference I fly to Seoul, which has become my second home. I keep returning to the exact same neighborhood and my 24-hour restaurant, because it’s a comfortable way to acclimate to the new time zone. It also allows me to get inexpensive dental work and buy a year’s worth of contact lenses for one-fifth the cost. From there I fly to Shenyang, a Chinese city in Manchuria I chose because I’m reading the classic novel by Cao Xueqin, “The Story of the Stone,”5 written during the Qing dynasty. That led me to reading about that period, which reminded me that after the Ming collapsed, forces from Manchuria, a different culture that became the Qing, took over China. I zeroed in on Shenyang, because it also has an interesting post-Qing history, especially during Communism, when it became a center of heavy manufacturing. Then it got clobbered by 1990s CCP economic reforms, mandated in the name of efficiency, making Zhu Rongji their Reagan, xiagang their neoliberalism, and Shenyang one of their Detroits.

This will be the sixth city I’ve visited in China, and I keep coming back because in each I’ve learned more than on almost any other trip. Understanding China is essential to understanding our current world — it’s not too much of an oversimplification to say there is the US model, and then China, and everything else is somewhere in between.

Even if current geopolitics isn’t your thing, China’s cultural richness is reason enough to keep going back. I’m embarrassed to admit that despite a lifelong interest in history, despite my father growing up in China, I knew/know very little about a civilization that stretches back three thousand years, complete with documentation, inventions, and artistic achievements that rival those of the West. China represents an equally successful, but very different, way of living that highlights the variations humans can achieve6.

From there I’m going to Naha, Okinawa, with a plan to make my way up to Kyushu via ferries, stopping in Tokunoshima and Amami Oshima along the way. Besides being a region of Japan I’ve never been to, I was also inspired by a fantastic book on the Imjin War, which sent me down many rabbit-holes, including one about the Ryukyu Kingdom. Even if I don’t see the legacy of that past during my walks — I’m sure I will see far, far more from the American occupation that transformed Japan post-WWII7 — just being there will encourage me to read more about it.

Also, as my equation says, comfort really matters to me (30% weighting!) and spending an hour in a public Japanese bath after a day walking is peak comfort to me. If there is a single experience from all my last five years of travels that I wish I could bottle up and carry home, it is Japanese bathing culture. Immersing yourself in a 105-degree pool, on the top floor of a Dormy Inn, the cityscape beneath transformed into a Monet painting by steamed-up windows, your body cleansed from fifteen minutes of fire-hose water pressure while sitting on a child-sized plastic stool, a minuscule towel on your head, and a cache of complimentary Popsicles waiting in a freezer for you, is the apogee of human civilization.

How do you pack for a trip?

Light, light, light, and if possible somehow lighter than that. Travel requires a great deal of displacement, of being between homes, lingering in the liminal, and the less you carry with you the less disruptive that feels. Nobody wants to be the person at the corner table cocooned behind a fortress of bags, everyone tripping on them, who has to muster an engineering corps to get across town to the airport.

While I’ve not changed that minimalist approach, I’ve changed my gear. I have two backpacks I switch between — both from Hyperlite. I have the Elevate 22L for shorter trips and the Windrider 40L for longer ones, or where I cross into different climates and need both warm and cold weather clothing.

They are expensive, but fantastic, with no internal structure so they maximize holding capacity, while minimizing weight. That can be annoying for some — who like various pouches and pockets — because it’s basically a big bag that straps to your back, but I make my own pockets by putting all my need-to-grab essentials (computer cords, bathroom supplies, papers, pens, glasses, etc.) in individual zip-lock bags that I roll up and tighten with a hair tie. (I am not being paid to hype any product mentioned!)

Below is a picture of everything I’m bringing for my upcoming trip, which I’ll be using the larger pack for since I need both cold and warm weather gear, and also need space to bring back Xmas presents!

I wear the bulkiest clothing — heavy sweater, winter jacket, and boots — and pack the rest. The only unnecessary items are the books, but I’ve tried e-readers and I simply don’t like them. I need at least one physical book, for those down times when the digital world is too much.

I effectively wear one outfit, and pack a single change, with enough socks and underwear to last a week (those are in the orange bag). If I need more clothing, I buy it where I am at, which has been a wonderful way to end up with odd fashion.

I also bring a trip’s supply of powdered electrolytes, which have saved me several times, from heat exhaustion, jet lag, and colds. Maybe it’s a placebo, but I don’t care since I believe in them.

What do you wear for walking?

This is the second most asked question, and I get it; shoes are important! I’ve been a Teva fanatic for seven years now, rocking the white-socks black-sandal look well before it became fashionable. Teva Hurricane XLT3 to be exact, pairs which have gotten me around the world multiple times, and lasted thousands of miles. Yet after several bouts of plantar fasciitis and rainy trips with soaking feet I switch between Tevas and a pair of Keen boots (Targhee).

I try to bring only one set of shoes, but on a trip like this, with snow in Shenyang and beaches in Okinawa, I’ll wear an old pair of Keens, then discard them after China.

I’m close to breaking up with my Keen boots, searching around for something more comfortable, and something that holds up better. On my last few pairs, chunks have come off the soles, which if you walk a lot means the death of a shoe, because the uneven wear means walking in a foot-injury machine.

So, suggestions are welcome!

That’s all well and good for you, but what about those of us who can only travel once a year?

I’m not delusional. I understand most people can’t travel weeks at a time, or have three hours a day to walk ten miles. I’ve got no problem with people packing in as many sights as possible in the limited time they have — going to see the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre, and then doing a boat ride on the Seine, returning home, and getting up at six a.m. to get their three-mile jog in before the kids wake up.

For those travelers with limited time, my simple advice is to take at least one day that’s not structured, and let yourself wander, especially into less touristy areas. Also, if you find a cafe, bar, or bistro that works for you, there is nothing wrong with going back a few more times. Or, take it easy and relax a little like you would at home. The stress of trying to maximize your experience can end up overwhelming everything else.

Then when you get home, open up your suitcases and see how many items you didn’t use. Almost always, there are several, and you could have packed half as lightly.

Regardless, if you ever have any questions, send me an email. Several people have taken me up on my offer to have a call with any subscriber who wants to chat about an upcoming trip! While I certainly can’t answer everything, or much of anything, I’ll do my best to help you work through the questions!

Until next week, enjoy!

PS: For those of you in Minneapolis, this Sunday, the 15th, I will be holding a meetup from 1 to 3 p.m. at the Arbeiter Brewing Company (3038 Minnehaha Ave) -- Come say hi, and have a beer on me!

1

They are where the locals with cross-border careers live, as well as ex-pats, and are the neighborhoods that draw the majority of tourists. Almost every country has at least one of them, and while I would probably live in one with my family if I were posted to work there, especially in third-world nations, and it’s often where I book my room, or at least on the edge of it, for convenience, it’s rare that I spend much time in them other than to sleep.

2

Obviously running is more time-efficient and not everyone has three spare hours every day to walk ten miles, but three miles or even one per day does wonders for your well-being. I don’t want to come off as an anti-jogging zealot — it’s a wonderful sport to keep fit, up to a certain point though. I found as I got older it took a toll on my body and I was spending more time dealing with injuries than I was running.

I used to say of the three triathlon sports, swimming was Communism (you had to trudge to a concrete institution, strip down to be observed, then share a pool with others, doing mind-numbing laps), cycling Capitalism (buy more and more expensive gear, to compete compete compete), and running Anarchy/Libertarianism (anyone could just do it, without constraint) and now that I’ve aged, I would say that walking is spiritualism (forget competition, forget goals, wander vagrantly, existing in the moment of your own thoughts).

3

Do not take boda-bodas. The hack motorcycle cabs that everyone in East Africa uses to get around, to weave in and out of traffic, to do everything, including carry bags, car bumpers, and even couches, a few miles, driven by testosterone-infused teenagers. In my hotel was an American surgeon who had grown up in Kampala. Every summer he spends two months leading a medical team (affiliated with his church) doing charity work. They were wonderful people, and I admired them to no end for spending weeks in rural communities providing free healthcare. When I mentioned the boda-bodas all of them told me how a high percentage of their work was for injuries — often serious — from boda-boda accidents. I wasn’t surprised by that at all.

For all my celebration of off-beat travel, that doesn’t mean I’m willing to take reckless risks, and being on a boda-boda that one time, where we (me, and the driver) almost got clipped by the front grille of a Ford truck (a medieval-war-looking contraption welded on in some back alley), peeking out into oncoming traffic, with only my knee grazing it at 45 mph, was enough for me. The image of me bleeding out in the dusty road, leg snapped, while a swarm of inquisitive kids poked me with sticks, “Hey Mister! You OK?” and the distant drone of the ambulance stuck in traffic a mile away grew louder as I slipped into unconsciousness, is not what I want to be my final one.

I kept ignoring this classic because I figured it was some dreary Eastern philosophy thing, but I was so wrong! It's funny, insightful, and reminds me of Vanity Fair -- a sprawling, rich book that's a joy to read.

This isn’t some ponderous metaphor for the stoic nobility of a heavenly stone imbued with godly powers. Rather, the stone is reborn as a dilettante boy who fritters away his youth while the family fortune drains away amid the decadence of a Qing household. It's as much a satire (on vanity, government corruption, etc.) as anything, but it's never confined to one genre. What it is not is dull.

I have to say, the marketing for the book isn't great. It screams boring, and it's not that at all.

6

Despite the differences, as I’ve written before I’m struck by the similarities at a deeper level, between Chinese Neo-Confucianism and Western Platonic thought. Classical Confucianism rose concurrently with Athenian dominance; Neo-Confucianism came roughly fifteen centuries later, though the parallels hold across both.

Both have a philosopher/sage class (guardians) at the top whose job is to build moral order. Both see human appetites, taken to excess, as corrupting, and argue for moderation and rationalism. Both see virtue achieved through study, with the guardians as teachers. Both are hierarchical, and conservative, with a functional society requiring proper order, again, enforced by the guardians.

7

Embracing Defeat is another fantastic book, this one about the American occupation of Japan, and how, as the title says, the Japanese, rather than simply submitting, seized on defeat to remake their nation with an alacrity that surprised everyone.
